newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Small rise in Australia business optimism - D&B.
newsitem.headline: Small rise in Australia business optimism - D&B.

text.p: Australian business executives have reported a small improvement in business optimism for June quarter, continuing the rise of the previous four quarters, according to a Dun & Bradstreet (D&B) survey.
"Business optimism in Australia has continued to rise with expectations for growth in orders and sales showing further improvements," D&B said in a commentary on the quarterly survey.

However expectations of further growth in profits, employment and capital investment have remained static. "The latest D&B survey indicates a mild recovery in the rate of growth of the Australian economy continuing in 1997," it said.
D&B economic consultant Duncan Ironmonger said the net proportion of firms actually raising prices peaked in March quarter 1995 and since then has declined to very low levels.
The fall in overall selling price expectations confirms a continuation of low inflation in Australia, he said.
"Executives have reduced selling price expectations, the mian factor being a fall in price expectations of non-durables manufacturers," said Ironmonger said.
The latest Australian national accounts released on March 5 showed the trend rate of inflation for domestic demand for the year to December 1996 was only 0.8 percent, he said.
Through the D&B survey showed actual profits results far below expectations, actual profit growth throughout 1996 was positive after two negative quarters in the second half of 1995.
"The net balance of actual profits growth returned to reasonable levels in wholesaling and non-durables manufacturing in the second half of 1996," Ironmonger said.
"However, the outlook for growth in profits in 1997 is still relatively weak in retailing in durables manufacturing."
The reversal of business expectations over the period from March quarter 1995 to March quarter 1996 reflected an economy that was slowing down quite quickly, he said.
The increase in the trend level of employment for the first half of 1995 was 30,000 per month and for the second half year the increase was only 11,000 per month.

In 1996 the trend level of employment fell slightly in February and March. Since then there has been a small rise of about 10,800 per month with an actual fall in full time employment in the last three months.

"The level of the D&B employment expectations index for the first two quarters of 1997 indicates that employment growth in the first half of 1997 will be positive but weak. The unemployment rate is unlikely to fall," Ironmonger said.

During 1995, in line with the majority of surveyed firms entering a profit growth recession in mid 1995, executives sharply reduced expectations of further increases in capital investment. This cut-back has taken greatest affect in retailing and in durables manufacturing.

From the low point of March quarter 1996, expectations for a growth in capital investment have increased in all sectors, and is now strongest in non-durables manufacturing in line with that sector's higher profits expectations.
The survey was conducted by Dun and Bradstreet in March.

About 900 business owners and senior executives representing major industry sectors were asked if they expected increases, decreases or no changes in quarterly sales, profits, orders, selling price, inventories, employment and capital investment.
(See separate item on detailed results of the survey)
